description:
AITHMAC is an initiative supported by the Mesopotamian Youth Society in Baghdad, Iraq. 

AITHMAC mission is to create autonomous robotic colonies in space that mine and use space resources to build entire habitats for humans to live in , and also to increase the manufacturing capability of the humankind , by manufacturing in space.

For Space Apps 2026, AITHMAC competes as a solo team.
summary:
SPOT is a free interactive website that lets anyone explore real NASA SPHEREx telescope images and see how the sky changes over time

Users can enter sky coordinates or select a target to view observations through interactive tools including image blinking, comparisons, difference imaging and timelines

We developed a system that processes and aligns SPHEREx observations directly from NASA’s public archives, allowing users to explore astronomical changes without installing specialized software

Our results include tracking Barnard’s Star across 16 years, following Pluto through 75 observations over eight days, studying stellar brightness variations and examining Pluto’s infrared spectrum

We also compare measurements with established astronomical references including Gaia and JPL Horizons to evaluate their accuracy

SPOT makes complex astronomical data accessible through a simple browser interface, helping students, researchers and curious people investigate the changing universe

Our goal is to turn publicly available space observations into an interactive experience that makes astronomical exploration more accessible to everyone
details:
Project Overview

SPOT stands for Sky Patches Over Time

We created SPOT to make astronomical observations easier to access, compare and understand

NASA’s SPHEREx mission provides valuable observations of the sky, but working with the original scientific files can require specialized tools and technical knowledge

SPOT transforms these observations into an interactive website where users can investigate changes in astronomical objects directly from their browsers

Main Features

  1. Search any region of the sky using right ascension and declination coordinates
  2. Explore observations through five comparison modes called Blink, Swipe, Difference, Timeline and Add All
  3. Adjust zoom and brightness while using a compass, scale bar and live coordinate display
  4. Explore seven prepared astronomical targets including Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis, Pluto and galaxy M101
  5. Generate observations for additional sky coordinates directly in the browser
  6. Access the original scientific files associated with the observations

Scientific Results

Barnard’s Star

We compared WISE observations from 2010 with SPHEREx observations from 2026

The measured displacement was 27.1 pixels compared with a predicted displacement of 27.3 pixels

WISE 0855

We measured a displacement of 20.7 pixels compared with a predicted displacement of 20.9 pixels

Because this object is faint and close to a background star, we consider the detection very likely rather than fully confirmed

Pluto

We analyzed 75 SPHEREx observations collected over eight days in October 2025

The measured positions agreed with JPL Horizons predictions within 1.05 pixels

We also examined Pluto’s infrared spectrum and identified reduced reflectance between 2.2 and 2.4 micrometers, consistent with published observations of methane ice

R Draconis

We observed brightness variations ranging from 0.46 to 1.98 times the median brightness

Using its known 246 day period, our fitted brightness maximum was approximately 10 days from the catalog prediction

RW Aurigae

Our analysis indicated a brightness decrease of approximately 1.7 to 1.9 times across wavelengths between 2.4 and 5 micrometers over one year

M101

We used galaxy M101 as a control target to evaluate our difference imaging system

Two regions were flagged across 18 difference images

Technical Development

We developed a Python processing pipeline using Astropy and reproject to work with SPHEREx Level 2 observations

During development, the IRSA search service returned errors, so we constructed our own searchable index containing 97,434 visits using information extracted from file headers

Our pipeline reads only the necessary sections of each scientific file, reducing typical data retrieval from approximately 65 MB to 2 MB

The system also performs background subtraction, masks flagged pixels and aligns observations with north facing upward

For scientifically meaningful comparisons, SPOT supports combining observations from the same detector and comparing frames within half a filter width of a selected wavelength

Difference imaging displays statistical significance to help distinguish meaningful changes from background noise

The website uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with GSAP and Lenis supporting the interface and animations

The project is hosted using GitHub Pages

Originality and Innovation

SPOT combines astronomical image processing, scientific validation and interactive visualization in a single publicly accessible platform

Instead of presenting telescope observations as static images, we allow users to explore how astronomical objects move and change over time

The platform connects real observations with reference measurements and provides direct access to original scientific files

We also included a clearly labeled Planet X simulation to demonstrate a hypothetical scenario without presenting simulated information as a real discovery

Intended Impact

Our goal is to make astronomical data more approachable for students, educators, researchers and the general public

SPOT allows users to explore real telescope observations without requiring specialized scientific software

We believe tools like SPOT can help more people engage with space science, understand astronomical observations and develop an interest in scientific investigation

Scientific Transparency

SPOT does not claim any new astronomical discoveries

We distinguish measured observations from predictions and simulations

We also acknowledge uncertainty when observations are difficult to interpret, particularly for faint objects such as WISE 0855

Our focus is accessibility, reproducibility and responsible scientific communication
